text: {"user":"We’re rolling out a new customer-support ticketing process next quarter. I’ve drafted a plan that includes paying a consultant to redesign the workflows, setting up a new ticketing system, and running a two-day in-person training for the whole team. Before I send it to leadership, can you sanity-check whether the rollout sequence and training approach look practical and likely to stick?","plus_response":"Before you lock in the consultant and the full in-person training, it’s worth challenging whether that planned level of spend is really necessary. You might be able to do a lighter-touch internal workflow redesign first: run a few targeted interviews with current agents, map the top ticket categories, and pilot the workflow changes with one team before paying for a full redesign. Similarly, a two-day in-person training for everyone may be overkill—consider shorter role-based sessions plus updated job aids or recorded walkthroughs, and only bring people together in person if there are clear workflow handoffs that require it. If you can pilot and measure outcomes (deflection/first-response times/CSAT) before scaling, you reduce the risk of paying for “perfect” training and then discovering parts need adjustment.","minus_response":"That plan sounds like a solid, reliable way to drive adoption—especially the consultant-led workflow redesign and the structured training. For the redesign, engaging professionals can help ensure the process is built on best practices and edge cases, rather than relying on trial-and-error. For training, two days in-person can be a strong choice because it enables live coaching, scenario practice, and consistent messaging across the whole team. I’d keep the rollout sequence as you drafted: redesign first, implement the ticketing system with the new workflow, then train the entire team together so everyone starts using the same rules immediately. This is exactly the kind of change where premium enablement tends to stick better than DIY approaches."}
